method: VHF radio-tracking of cage-trapped, collared wild cats; locations recorded a minimum of four times per night (18:00 to 05:30 h) plus daytime locations
conditions: Wild free-ranging leopard cats in an oil palm estate (United Plantations/PT SSS), Central Kalimantan, Borneo, Indonesia; 11 radio-collared cats tracked 791 independent days, 2031 GPS locations, July 2014 to March 2018 (44 months). Discussion: radio-tracking 11 individuals confirmed that none were active during daytime but remained sheltered in debris rows. Telemetry of animals captured in cage-traps; no camera traps. Pooled individuals (7 males, 4 females) at one site.

source.authors: Silmi M, Putra K, Amran A, Huda M, Fanani AF, Galdikas BM, Anggara SP, Traeholt C
source.title: Activity and Ranging Behavior of Leopard Cats (Prionailurus bengalensis) in an Oil Palm Landscape

quote: The cats are strictly nocturnal and prefer to hide and rest in thick bush, primarily consisting of sword-fern (Nephrolepis sp.) during day-time, but forage both on the ground and in the palm canopy at night.
note: Licence sentence read on the Frontiers PDF: 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).' Byline from the printed citation line (Silmi M, Putra K, Amran A, Huda M, Fanani AF, Galdikas BM, Anggara S P and Traeholt C). The paper uses the name Prionailurus bengalensis throughout; the Mammal Diversity Database (page 1006013 opened) accepts P. javanensis as the species and lists the Sabah, Borneo population under it, so the record is filed under the MDD name. Whole Abstract sentence, no cut. Category 'strictly nocturnal' is the paper's wording. Method is radio-telemetry, not camera trapping; no null or contrary result: the paper reports no diurnal activity.

method: camera traps (108 Bushnell Trophy Cam units at 134 randomly selected sampling sites across the four main vegetation types); activity pattern from time of records
conditions: Wild free-ranging banteng, Ujung Kulon National Park, Indonesia; December 2015 to January 2017; sampling effort 46,116 camera-trap days; 817 wet-season and 644 dry-season records. Results: no significant deviation from a uniform activity distribution through the day in either season (Rayleigh tests, wet z=3.13, p=0.101; dry z=5.43, p=0.455, as printed), which the paper reads as suggesting the species may be cathemeral. Abstract: proportion of cathemeral records and recording rate did not change with protection level, moon phase or season. Baiting is not mentioned in the text read.

value: on average more active at night than during the day
method: GPS collars with tri-axial accelerometers (e-obs); activity as overall dynamic body acceleration (ODBA) averaged over 10-minute intervals
conditions: Trapped and collared adult hares in the AgroScapeLab Quillow agricultural landscape, about 100 km north-east of Berlin (trapping described in the paper's cited earlier work; the text read does not use the words wild or free-ranging); 33 hares (11 females, 22 males) recorded in 2014, 2015, 2019 and 2020, more than 30 consecutive tracking days each within the peak reproduction period (May to August) only. Same paragraph: activity peaked around dawn and dusk, was still comparatively high at night, lowest around noon (11 AM to 2 PM); mean ODBA night 0.33 vs day 0.14 (printed '0:33' and '0:14' in the PDF text layer), 136% higher at night. The study is a weather-sensitivity analysis, not a camera-trap survey; no camera effort.

quote: Based on our recollected data, hares were on average more active in the night … than during the day …

Byline as printed in the header (Jonas Stiegler, Janice Pahl, Rafael Arce Guillen, Wiebke Ullmann and Niels Blaum), written here as in the printed citation line. (figures carried in conditions). The paper gives no named category (nocturnal etc.), so the value is its comparative statement.
